rashi:a1.1: But a blemished one is permitted: and it is Rabbi Yosei, who said that where he slaughtered it the Rabbis permit [the wool]; or else it is Akavya, [who permits it] even though [an expert] did not deem it permitted. And this is difficult for Reish Lakish.
rashi:a1.2: It calls it unblemished: and what does “even though a blemish developed in it” mean? Even though it was afterward shown to a Sage and he said it is a permanent blemish.
gershom:a1.1: But a blemished one is permitted: [if this is so where one] plucked, all the more so [where the wool] shed.
gershom:a2.1: And even though an expert did not deem it permitted: beforehand, but only after it shed.
gershom:a3.1: Reish Lakish said to him: this tanna of “one who plucks wool” calls it unblemished wherever an expert did not deem it permitted before he plucked, for it is like plucking from an unblemished one; so one cannot say, “but a blemished one is permitted.” [Rabbeinu Gershom puts this answer in Reish Lakish’s mouth; the daf gives it in the Gemara’s voice.] (The printed text adds: “that became impure,” that is, that became blemished.)
rashi:a2.1: Let us say: that this [statement] of Reish Lakish is the subject of a dispute between tanna’im.
rashi:a2.2: Prohibited: for with an unblemished one even Akavya concedes, since people would come to keep it [alive] and to strip it of its sanctity for the altar; moreover, it does not yet have any permission at all. And although it uses [the word] “plucks,” the same applies to [wool] that was torn out [by itself], as is explained at the end of the discussion.
tosafot:a2.1: A blemished firstborn from which one plucked: here it does not teach “and placed it in a compartment,” because one who plucks is wicked and intends to benefit at once; but where it shed, it does teach “and placed it in a compartment.”
rashi:a2.3: Not in this: [the case] where it died, did Akavya permit, but where he slaughtered it.
rashi:a3.1: Rabbi Yosei said: My father concedes: whose name was Ḥalafta, who is one of the Sages who disagree with Akavya, and he concedes in this [case], where he slaughtered it, that it is permitted.
gershom:a4.1: My father Ḥalafta concedes in this [case], where he slaughtered it, that it is permitted, even according to the Sages.
rashi:a3.2: But be’yiḥud the Sages said: that truly and clearly the Sages said one should place the hair of a blemished firstborn that shed in a compartment.
rashi:a3.3: Aval: [means] truly; and a parallel to it is in Eruvin, in the chapter Bakol Me’arvin (Eruvin 38a), at its end.
rashi:a3.4: Be’yiḥud: clearly; and a parallel to it is in tractate Yoma (54a): “And they knew be’yiḥud that the Ark was hidden there.”
rashi:a3.5: Perhaps there is hope: perhaps it will become permitted to derive benefit [from it]. And he explains what hope there is: that if he slaughters it, all agree it is permitted.
gershom:a5.1: But be’yiḥud they said: this aval is like “truly,” as it is written: “Aval we are guilty” (Genesis 42:21). Be’yiḥud: clearly.
gershom:a6.1: And he places it in a compartment, for it has a remedy: if he slaughters it, it will be permitted.
rashi:a4.1: Rabbi Yosei is the same as the first tanna: who said, “One who plucks wool from an unblemished firstborn and slaughtered it, it is prohibited”; by inference, [wool plucked from] a blemished one that he slaughtered is permitted according to all, and they disagree where it died. In Rabbi Yosei’s “concedes” too they disagree where it died, and according to the first tanna as well they disagree where it died.
gershom:a7.1: On what did they disagree etc.: Rabbi Yosei, who said they disagreed where it died, is the same as the first tanna, who said they disagree where it died.
rashi:a5.1: The first tanna holds: if an expert deemed it permitted, yes; if not, no: for you must explain it this way, just as you explained it for Reish Lakish above, when we raised an objection to him from the first clause of the first tanna’s words, which teaches “one who plucks wool from an unblemished firstborn,” implying that a blemished one is permitted, and Reish Lakish answered: wherever an expert did not deem it permitted, he calls it unblemished. Evidently this is the meaning of his words: one who plucks wool from an unblemished firstborn, that is, a blemished one that an expert did not deem permitted, it is prohibited according to all; but a blemished firstborn, that is, one an expert deemed permitted, from which one plucked etc. And Rabbi Yosei holds that even though an expert did not deem it permitted when it shed, the Rabbis permit it. From where [do we know this]? From his saying “there is hope,” which implies there is hope that an expert will deem it permitted and he will slaughter it; by inference, an expert had not yet deemed it permitted when it shed. [Rashi, like Rabbeinu Gershom, attributes the earlier answer to Reish Lakish; the daf gives it in the Gemara’s voice.]
tosafot:a5.1: For the first tanna holds: if an expert deemed it permitted, yes; if not, no: The Kuntres [Rashi] explained that since we answered above that wherever an expert did not deem it permitted he calls it unblemished, the latter clause, which calls it blemished, speaks of [an animal] an expert deemed permitted. But this is difficult for his explanation: the reason [the Gemara] answered so above was in order to establish Reish Lakish according to everyone; but now that we must say, in either case, that it is a dispute of tanna’im, it is more reasonable to say the reverse, so that the words of the first tanna stand according to their plain meaning. It seems [better] to explain that the Talmud now holds so because Rabbi Yosei says “perhaps there is hope”: he would not have said this with reference to slaughter, which is in the owner’s own hands, so there is no “perhaps” about it; rather, he says “perhaps there is hope” with reference to an expert’s permission, that a Sage may attend to him and deem it permitted, and that is not so certain a thing, for who says an expert will attend to him? Nevertheless, in the conclusion [the Gemara] says “perhaps there is hope” refers to slaughter.
gershom:a8.1: The first tanna holds: what Akavya permits where it died is [only] where an expert deemed it permitted before the hair was plucked. And Rabbi Yosei comes to say, for every later tanna adds something, that even though an expert did not deem it permitted beforehand but only afterward [after it was plucked], Akavya permits it. And so it is a dispute of tanna’im.
gershom:a9.1: No, everyone agrees that if an expert deemed it permitted: before the plucking, yes; if not, no; and they do not disagree about this. Rather, there are three disputes in the matter.
rashi:a6.1: They disagree where it died, and the same applies where he slaughtered it: since we do not find in the words of the first tanna that he says that where he slaughtered it all agree it is permitted.
gershom:a10.1: For the first tanna holds that they disagree where it died, and the same is true where he slaughtered it: since he said nothing about [a case] where he slaughtered it, we must say that he holds they disagree in both.
rashi:a8.1: The halakha is in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda: that they disagree where he slaughtered it, and not where it died.
gershom:a11.1: The halakha is in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda: that Akavya permits only where he slaughtered it.
gershom:a12.1: Bivḥirta [in our preferred tractate]: tractate Eduyot.
gershom:a13.1: Wool that is medublal: [that is,] medouldal, dangling.
gershom:a14.1: That appears with the fleece: what appears attached to the fleece is permitted.
rashi:a10.1: This and that: whether it appears or does not appear, it is permitted, for Rabbi Yosei said that even [wool] placed in a compartment the Rabbis too permit where he slaughtered it.
gershom:a15.1: This and that: whether it appears or does not appear [with the fleece], as we said that where he slaughtered it, all agree it is permitted.
rashi:a11.1: If the Rabbis, both this and that are prohibited: for what is attached to it requires burial according to all, and what is detached from it the Rabbis prohibit, even [wool] placed in a compartment.
gershom:a16.1: If the Rabbis, both this and that are prohibited: even [the hairs] that were plucked earlier, and all the more so what was plucked afterward, since death renders it prohibited.
gershom:a17.1: And if Akavya, it should be the reverse: for when he permits where it died, he permits only what shed beforehand, but what shed after it died is prohibited according to all. So it should have taught: what does not appear is permitted, and what appears is prohibited.
rashi:a12.1: Rather, it is obvious that it is Rabbi Yehuda: who said they disagree where he slaughtered it.
rashi:a12.2: This and that: whether it appears or does not appear.
rashi:a13.1: And conclude from it that they disagree where he slaughtered it: since you cannot establish it in any other way. And since [the mishna] taught us anonymously in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda, conclude from it that the halakha is in accordance with him.
gershom:a18.1: Rather, is it not the Rabbis: who, where he slaughtered it, prohibit what shed beforehand; but after it was slaughtered, the hide and what is attached to it are permitted. And that is what it says: what appears with the fleece is permitted, for it calls the wool attached to the hide “fleece”; and what does not appear is prohibited.
rashi:a14.1: One who plucks wool from an unblemished burnt offering: [plucked] during its life; according to the Rabbis, what is [the halakha]? About [wool of] a blemished one, after slaughter, you need not ask, for according to the Rabbis it is certainly prohibited: if you permit it, one will come to keep it [alive] and come to [violate the prohibitions of] shearing and labor.
tosafot:a14.1: In brief: One version of Rashi’s commentary reads [the case as one where the burnt offering] “became blemished, was afterward redeemed, and he slaughtered it,” to make it resemble a firstborn, with the plucking done while it was unblemished. Tosafot ask: such wool would itself need to be stood and valuated [before redemption], and standing the animal does not help for the wool, as is evident in Reshit HaGez (Ḥullin 135a). They answer: (1) he holds like Reish Lakish, who says in the second chapter of Temura (32b) that according to the Rabbis altar offerings were not included in standing and valuation, and Rav holds the same in chapter two (above, Bekhorot 15a); (2) with altar offerings, which have inherent sanctity, the wool is subordinate to the animal, even what was plucked, unlike consecrated property for Temple maintenance; or (3) this wool is regarded as if from a blemished animal from the outset. They compare the shofar of a burnt offering, with which one fulfills the obligation because it becomes non-sacred through misuse (Rosh HaShana 28a), or which is explained as an animal consecrated for its value (compare Pesaḥim 27b). Still, Tosafot ask: if the wool needs redemption anyway, what would the owner gain by keeping the animal, so why decree? They suggest instead that the case is a burnt offering slaughtered for the altar, whose blood sprinkling permits the hide to the priests, and the question is whether wool torn out [during its life] is also permitted by it. But this depends on a dispute of amora’im in HaMizbe’aḥ Mekadesh (Zevaḥim 86a) on bones that separated before sprinkling: Rabbi Zeira holds sprinkling permits them, while Rabbi Elazar holds one is liable for misusing them, which Rashi there explains as forever; though some texts there read “until sprinkling.” Open on Sefaria for the full text.
gershom:a19.1: From an unblemished burnt offering: about a blemished one of other consecrated animals he does not ask, since it can be redeemed one does not keep it, but redeems it and slaughters it at once; therefore it is permitted. And some say: since it requires an expert, there is certainly concern that one will keep them, and he does not ask. Rather, he asks about an unblemished one.
rashi:a14.2: Is there anyone who permits it: according to the Rabbis? This one is certainly a wicked person.
tosafot:a14.2: Plucks: is there anyone who permits it? The Kuntres [Rashi] explained: according to the Rabbis, this one is certainly a wicked person. This implies that according to Akavya it might be permitted, although in truth, according to Akavya too it is prohibited with an unblemished animal, as is evident from the baraita “one who plucks wool from an unblemished firstborn.” Nevertheless the Kuntres explained it so because, even without that baraita, it is a simple matter that according to the Rabbis, at least, [wool one] plucked is prohibited.
gershom:a20.1: Wool that was torn out: by itself. Of a sin offering and a guilt offering etc.; of a firstborn and tithe, too, you need not ask: according to all it is prohibited, since they do not come for atonement, and one keeps them out of desire for the wool that sheds, and comes to a stumbling.
gershom:a21.1: When you raise the dilemma, it is about a burnt offering: since it does not come for atonement, for it is merely a gift, one keeps it.
rashi:b1.1: Since its primary [function] is not to come for atonement: for one does not bring it for a sin.
rashi:b1.2: Since it atones for a positive [mitzva]: for a burnt offering atones for a positive mitzva, as we say in tractate Yoma (36a): over a burnt offering one confesses the sin of [neglecting] gleanings, forgotten sheaves and pe’a.
gershom:b1.1: Or perhaps: since it atones for a positive mitzva, for we say that it comes for a positive mitzva and for a prohibition that is rectified by a positive mitzva.
gershom:b2.1: For with a blemished one even plucking is permitted: but not with an unblemished one.
rashi:b4.1: But didn’t we learn “shed”: evidently Akavya permits [wool] that shed, and not [wool] that was plucked.
gershom:b3.1: But didn’t we learn “shed”: with a blemished one, and not “plucks.”
gershom:b4.1: It taught “shed” to convey the far-reaching nature of the Rabbis: that they prohibit even [wool] that shed by itself; but in truth, the same is true for Akavya, that he permits even plucking.
gershom:b5.1: It taught “plucks” to convey the far-reaching nature of Akavya: who permits [it] with slaughter.
rashi:b5.1: Whose root is turned toward its head: that is folded in its middle, so that its two ends are seen outside.
gershom:b6.1: Any whose root: of the hair is plucked, and the root is turned toward its head and its head is near the skin: it appears that it was plucked during [the animal’s] life.
rashi:b5.2: That is not compressed: that is not level with the fleece but is seen rising upward.
gershom:b7.1: That is not compressed with the fleece: that is, it is not attached, lying level with the rest of the fleece, but is plucked and sticks out almost outside the rest of the fleece.
rashi:b6.1: What is the reason he did not state in accordance with Rav Natan: for certainly, since it is not compressed, “does not appear with the fleece” applies to it.
rashi:b6.2: Because it is impossible for any fleece to be without dangling hairs: that rise upward, and if in such a case it were prohibited, you would have no permitted fleece. Rabbi Natan [the daf: Rav Natan bar Oshaya] is the more stringent; that is why [the Gemara] does not ask, “What is the reason he did not state in accordance with Reish Lakish?”
gershom:b8.1: He holds: this too, whose root is turned toward its head but does not stick out beyond the rest of the fleece, is “appearing with the fleece.” Reish Lakish holds that [hair] whose root is turned certainly does not appear with the fleece, more than that which is not compressed, for that is the way of fleece, since it is impossible for fleece to be without dangling hairs.
rashi:b7.1: We will return to you, HaLoke’aḥ Behema [the end of chapter 3].
gershom:b9.1: We will return to you, HaLoke’aḥ [Behema].
rashi:b8.1: Mishna. Until when [must an Israelite] tend to the firstborn: nowadays, before he gives it to the priest, for he is obliged to keep it with him whether he wishes or not, and to feed it.
tosafot:b8.1: Mishna. With a small animal, thirty days: there is a dispute like this one concerning tending a lost item (Bava Metzia 28).
gershom:b10.1: Israelites are obligated to tend to the firstborn: that is, until when is an Israelite obligated to raise the firstborn before he gives it to the priest.
gershom:b11.1: With a small animal, thirty days, and with a large one, fifty days: as is explained in the Gemara.
rashi:b8.2: He may not give it: it is explained in the Gemara.
gershom:b12.1: If the priest said to him within that period, “Give it to me,” he may not give it: for he appears like a priest who assists at the threshing floors, to whom one may not give teruma, since it appears as if it was given to him as his wages. Here too it appears as if he gives it to him for that benefit, that he took his place in tending it.
rashi:b8.3: If it was blemished and he said to him: [that is,] the priest [said] within that period, “Give it to me so I may eat it,” it is permitted.
gershom:b13.1: And if, within the period, when a blemish developed in it, he said to him, “Give it to me so I may eat it” at once, it is permitted: since the priest does not need to keep it, he does not appear like one who assists. But in an ordinary case he may not give it to him, for he cannot eat it at once, until a blemish develops in it, when the Temple is not standing.
rashi:b9.1: Whether unblemished: when the Temple is standing.
gershom:b14.1: From where are these matters derived: that he is obligated to tend to it for thirty days.
rashi:b11.1: Gemara. “The fullness of your harvest and the outflow of your presses” etc.: and next to it, “So you shall do with your oxen, with your sheep” etc. We interpret it thus: “The firstborn of your sons you shall give to Me,” and so “with your sheep”: just as the mitzva of the firstborn of your sons is after thirty [days], as it is written: “And those that are to be redeemed of them, from a month old you shall redeem” (Numbers 18:15–16), so too the firstborn of the flock, after thirty. “The fullness of your harvest and the outflow of your presses,” that is, first fruits; so too “with your oxen”: just as first fruits are after fifty [days], for the grain ripens at Passover and first fruits are not brought until the two loaves are brought at Atzeret [Shavuot], as we say in the chapter Rabbi Yishmael (Menaḥot 68b).
tosafot:b11.1: “You shall not delay the fullness of your harvest and the outflow of your presses…so you shall do with your oxen”: that is, fifty days, from the day the omer is brought on Passover, which completes the ripening of the grain, until Atzeret, when the two loaves are brought to permit the new grain in the Temple. And if you say: this is on the fiftieth day, and it is not like “the firstborn of your sons… [so you shall do with] your sheep,” which is after thirty [days]. [The printed text gives no answer.]
gershom:b15.1: For the verse states: “The firstborn of your sons you shall give to Me,” and of your sons it is written: “From a month old you shall redeem” (Numbers 18:16); “so you shall do with your sheep” as well. “You shall not delay the fullness of your harvest and your outflow”: and we read in the Mekhilta: “Your fullness” — these are the first fruits, which are taken from the full [crop]; “and your outflow” — this is teruma. (A footnote in the printed text suggests: “this is teruma, which renders the grain a mixture [meduma]”, in the words of “my teacher the Gaon.”) And with first fruits we hold that one brings and recites… (The printed text here is garbled.) …that one brings and recites, that is, from Passover until Atzeret, which is fifty days; “so you shall do with your oxen”: tend to it fifty days.
gershom:b16.1: Reverse it: let me say, “The firstborn of your sons you shall give to Me… so you shall do with your oxen.”
rashi:b12.1: The earlier to the earlier: “the fullness of your harvest and the outflow of your presses” come first in the first verse; therefore we apply them to “your oxen,” which comes first in the second verse.
rashi:b12.2: And the later: “the firstborn of your sons,” which comes later in the first verse, we apply to “your sheep,” which comes later in the second verse.
gershom:b17.1: It stands to reason, the earlier to the earlier: “your fullness,” which is earlier in the verse, is juxtaposed with “your oxen,” which is earlier than “your sheep”; and “the firstborn of your sons,” which comes after “your fullness,” with “your sheep,” which comes after “your oxen.”
rashi:b12.3: The adjacent to the adjacent: and “the firstborn of your sons” is adjacent to “your oxen.”
gershom:b18.1: The adjacent to the adjacent: “the firstborn of your sons” is adjacent to “your oxen.”
gershom:b19.1: The verse states, “[so] you shall do with your oxen”: that “you shall do” is not needed at all, except to add [an extra] doing for your oxen beyond your sheep.
rashi:b14.1: And say sixty: for we require another “doing” like this one of “the firstborn of your sons.”
gershom:b20.1: And say sixty: since it added, let it say twice [the time] of your sheep, that is, sixty.
rashi:b14.2: The verse gave it over only to the Sages: since it did not reveal to you the measure of the doing you should add, it certainly gave it over to the Sages to explain the reasoning to you, and you shall follow them.
gershom:b21.1: The verse gave it over only to the Sages: that is, it did not say sixty, double [the time] for sheep; rather it is the Sages who explain fifty days, and they relied on “you shall not delay the fullness of your harvest and your outflow.”
rashi:b16.2: Because its teeth are small: and it cannot eat grass, and if it is not with its mother it will die.
gershom:b22.1: Because its teeth are small: and it cannot eat well until three months.
rashi:b17.1: Because he appears like a priest who assists at the threshing floors: for nowadays a firstborn is not fit for anything until a blemish develops in it; and since it falls on the Israelite to tend to it for fifty days, if the priest said to him within that period, “Give it to me and I will feed it,” then even though he gave him no [real] benefit, he is like one who hires him and saves him the trouble, on condition that he gives it to him and not to another priest. So he is like a priest who assists at the threshing floors, threshing and winnowing so that they will give him the terumot. But if it was blemished and he said, “Give it to me so I may eat it,” since it is fit for him, he is not like a priest who assists.
rashi:b18.1: In the home of the shepherds: refers to the priests, so that [the owners] will give them the firstborn animals.
rashi:b18.2: At the threshing floors: refers to all of them: the priests on account of teruma, the Levites on account of the first tithe, and the poor on account of the tithe for the poor.
rashi:b18.3: In the slaughterhouse: refers to the priests, on account of the foreleg, the jaw and the maw.
gershom:b23.1: The priests who assist in the home of the shepherds: to guard or to feed [the flock], so that they will give them the firstborn animals; and Levites and poor people [who assist] at the threshing floors, on account of the first tithe and the tithe for the poor; and the priests who assist in the slaughterhouse, for the sake of the gifts.
gershom:b24.1: And if they did so: that they gave [these] to them as their wages.
gershom:b25.1: They desecrated: they turned the teruma and the tithe into non-sacred produce that has no law of sanctity; they did not act well and did not fulfill their obligation, and there is a sin [punishable by] death in the matter.
tosafot:b19.1: And if you would say: not death, [come and hear] etc.: not precisely, for it is not counted in the chapter Elu Hen HaNisrafin (Sanhedrin 83a) among those [liable to] death [at the hand of Heaven]; rather, it is close to a sin [punishable by] death.
gershom:b26.1: [To separate] teruma and tithes a second time, in full.
rashi:b20.2: From the exempt for the obligated: for perhaps they will have two se’a, one fully untithed and one from which [teruma] was separated [and given] to the priest who assists. If you tell him that it reverts and he must separate [teruma] from it as a penalty, the householder will think it is fully untithed and will separate from it for the other one, though by Torah law it is exempt and [the second separation] is only a penalty.
tosafot:b20.1: Perhaps he will come to separate from the exempt for the obligated etc.: In several places we say, “[It is] teruma, and he must separate teruma again,” and there we do not make this decree, because the first teruma goes to the priest, so he knows that the second is rabbinic. And even if he had already given the first to the priest before a Sage told him to separate again, nevertheless, since the priest does not return the first to him, he knows that the second is rabbinic. But here he thinks he gave it to the priest as wages for his help, and [so] the priest keeps it. And in several places one must draw distinctions in such matters, such as in Pesaḥim at the beginning of Makom SheNahagu (Pesaḥim 51a), about those who separated ḥalla from rice, where we said that if most people do not eat rice, a non-priest should eat it in front of them, lest they come to separate from the exempt for the obligated; and in the first chapter of Yoma (10a), about the sukka of the festival being obligated, on the festival, in eruv, mezuza and tithe, where it says there that it speaks by Torah law, for if [the obligation were] rabbinic, perhaps one would come to separate from the exempt for the obligated; and with demai, one who buys from a gentile, according to the one who holds that [a gentile] has ownership [in the Land of Israel], the Sages obligated him [to tithe] and were not concerned about this.
gershom:b27.1: Rather, because perhaps he would come to separate from the exempt for the obligated: for if we obligated him to separate another teruma, this man would think that all this grain is definitely untithed, as if no teruma had been separated from it at all. And if he has other produce that is definitely untithed, he would come to separate for it from this grain, from which he already gave and which was already exempted (for he would think that we required him to separate another teruma not as a penalty but as a full obligation), and so he would come to separate from the exempt for the obligated. Therefore we do not penalize him.
